purpose: Interactive beginner layer for the Hays/Kyle Soil Habitat Translator. It turns goals, site observations, simple backyard tests, and season into plain first actions.
important_limit: This is a habitat and garden decision aid, not a fertilizer prescription, engineering report, or exact microbe test.

goals.label: Plant native flowers
first_actions: Start with a small bed you can water during establishment.
Use a mix of native grasses and flowering perennials.
Keep soil covered between young plants with leaves, mulch, or nurse plants.
avoid: Do not over-amend the whole bed before you know the soil habitat.
Do not choose only showy flowers; include grasses or structure plants.
goals.bed_structure: Aim for about 50-60% flowering perennials, 30-40% native grasses/sedges, and 5-10% shrubs or accents.

goals.label: Fix a struggling bed
goals.plain_goal: Figure out why plants are stressed before buying more fertilizer.
first_actions: Check soil moisture 4 inches deep before watering again.
Look for compaction, crusting, shallow rock, or water sitting after rain.
Use the map and one backyard test before changing fertilizer.
avoid: Do not assume yellow leaves always mean low nitrogen.
Do not add sand to clay soil.
Do not till repeatedly as the first fix.
goals.bed_structure: Start with soil repair and observation. Replant with tough native anchors only after the stress pattern is clearer.

goals.label: Reduce watering
goals.plain_goal: Make the garden better at handling heat and dry spells.
first_actions: Keep soil shaded with plants, mulch, or leaf litter.
Use deep-rooted local natives matched to clay, limestone, or shallow soil.
Water new plants slowly and deeply, then stretch time between waterings.
avoid: Do not water daily and shallow unless seedlings require it.
Do not leave bare soil exposed through summer.
goals.bed_structure: Use drought-tolerant native perennials, bunchgrasses, and shrubs in repeated clusters rather than scattered single plants.

goals.label: Start a lawn alternative
goals.plain_goal: Replace high-input turf with a lower-water native ground layer.
first_actions: Decide whether the area needs to handle foot traffic or can become meadow-like.
Use soil habitat to choose clay prairie, rocky savanna, or shade-tolerant species.
Convert in phases so weeds and erosion stay manageable.
avoid: Do not seed into dense turf without site prep.
Do not expect a meadow to look like a lawn during establishment.
goals.bed_structure: For meadow-style areas, use native grasses as the matrix and add forbs in patches. For paths, keep durable groundcovers or mulch routes.

goals.label: Plant trees or shrubs
goals.plain_goal: Choose woody plants that match root depth, drainage, limestone, and heat.
first_actions: Check soil depth and drainage before choosing tree size.
Protect the root zone from compaction.
Mulch wide and shallow, not piled against the trunk.
avoid: Do not plant water-loving trees on shallow rocky uplands.
Do not bury the root flare.
Do not amend only a tiny planting hole in heavy clay.
goals.bed_structure: Use a layered planting: canopy or small tree, shrubs, grasses/sedges, and leaf-litter-tolerant perennials.

goals.label: Slow runoff or erosion
goals.plain_goal: Help stormwater soak in and protect soil from washing away.
first_actions: Keep bare soil covered immediately.
Use roots to slow water: grasses, sedges, and deep-rooted perennials.
Place mulch, logs, rocks, or plants across the slope contour where appropriate.
avoid: Do not leave slopes bare after disturbance.
Do not send concentrated runoff into a new loose bed without protection.
goals.bed_structure: Build a dense root mat with native grasses/sedges first, then add flowers and shrubs once the soil is stable.

goals.label: Just understand my soil
goals.plain_goal: Learn what your soil habitat means before making big changes.
first_actions: Look up the soil on the map.
Do one simple backyard test: ribbon, infiltration, or shovel test.
Compare what the map says with what you see in the garden.
avoid: Do not make expensive changes from one clue alone.
Do not treat regional microbe data as an exact yard test.
goals.bed_structure: No planting structure needed yet. Learn the habitat first, then choose plants.

observations.label: Water sits after rain
observations.means: Water is entering slowly, the soil is already full, the soil is compacted, or the site is in a low spot.
observations.first_step: Do an infiltration test and avoid walking or working this area while wet.
observations.avoid: Do not add more water until you check moisture below the surface.

observations.label: Soil cracks when dry
observations.means: Clay soils can shrink when dry and swell when wet. Roots need plants that tolerate wet-dry swings.
observations.first_step: Keep the surface covered and use deep-rooted native plants that can handle clay cycles.
observations.avoid: Do not till repeatedly to break cracks; it can make structure worse over time.

observations.label: Soil is sticky when wet
observations.means: Sticky soil often has high clay. Clay is not bad, but it is easy to damage when wet.
observations.first_step: Wait until it is moist, not sticky, before planting or digging.
observations.avoid: Do not work clay soil while it sticks to tools or shoes.

observations.label: Soil is shallow or rocky
observations.means: Roots may have less room and the site may dry quickly after rain.
observations.first_step: Choose smaller, drought-adapted native plants and protect the thin soil layer.
observations.avoid: Do not choose plants that need deep, constantly moist soil.

observations.label: Leaves turn yellow easily
observations.means: Yellow leaves can come from high-pH limestone soil, water stress, root stress, or true nutrient shortage.
observations.first_step: Check moisture and soil pH before fertilizing.
observations.avoid: Do not guess with fertilizer before checking root and water conditions.

observations.label: Plants wilt even after watering
observations.means: Water may not be reaching active roots, or roots may lack air in compacted or saturated soil.
observations.first_step: Check soil moisture 4 inches deep and inspect whether the root zone is soggy, dry, or compacted.
observations.avoid: Do not keep watering daily if the soil below is already wet.

observations.label: Plants die in summer heat
observations.means: Bare soil, shallow roots, wrong plant choice, or poor establishment can make heat stress worse.
observations.first_step: Cover soil, water new plants deeply, and shift planting to fall when possible.
observations.avoid: Do not plant tender or water-hungry species into full summer stress.

observations.label: Plants grow fast but flop
observations.means: Plants may be getting too much water/fertility, too little sun, or the wrong species for the soil.
observations.first_step: Reduce pampering and use locally adapted natives with natural structure.
observations.avoid: Do not keep adding fertilizer to make weak growth stronger.

observations.label: Bare soil gets hard or crusty
observations.means: Rain impact and sun can seal the surface, especially on bare clay or silty soil.
observations.first_step: Add plant cover, leaf litter, or mulch and keep traffic off wet soil.
observations.avoid: Do not leave exposed soil through hot months or heavy rain periods.

observations.label: Nothing wants to grow
observations.means: The problem may be compaction, construction fill, shallow rock, wrong plant match, water pattern, or shade/sun mismatch.
observations.first_step: Do a shovel test and a moisture check before replanting.
observations.avoid: Do not keep replacing plants without identifying the site stress.

do: Keep soil covered so clay does not bake into a crust.
Use deep-rooted native grasses and forbs to build pores over time.
Plant when clay is moist but not sticky.
avoid: Do not add sand to clay.
Do not repeatedly till wet clay.

do: Use plants that tolerate short wet periods if the site truly stays wet.
Keep equipment and foot traffic off saturated soil.
Watch whether water sits because of a low spot, compaction, or true floodplain position.
avoid: Do not plant dry-upland species in a spot that stays saturated.

do: Water slowly so it can soak in instead of running off.
Use roots and mulch to improve surface structure.
avoid: Do not blast water onto bare soil.

do: Create walking paths so beds are not stepped on.
Use living roots and mulch to rebuild structure.
Loosen only where needed for planting, then protect the area.
avoid: Do not drive or walk repeatedly over wet soil.

do: Use local drought-adapted natives.
Water new plants deeply and less often after establishment begins.
Plant in fall when possible.
avoid: Do not leave soil bare in summer.

do: Choose plants that naturally grow in rocky or thin soils.
Expect smaller mature size and slower establishment.
Protect existing topsoil from erosion.
avoid: Do not force deep-rooted water-loving plants into thin soil.

do: Choose limestone-adapted Central Texas natives.
Use organic cover and roots to help nutrient cycling.
Use soil testing before adding phosphorus or iron products.
avoid: Do not try to permanently turn limestone soil acidic.

do: Look for plants adapted to high-pH soil.
Check whether yellow leaves are from pH, water, or root stress.
avoid: Do not assume yellow leaves are always fertilizer shortage.

do: Cover bare soil with native plants, mulch, leaves, or temporary nurse plants.
Keep living roots in the ground across more of the year.
avoid: Do not leave bare soil exposed during heat or heavy rain.

do: Plant across the slope to slow water.
Use grasses, sedges, and mulch to protect the soil surface.
Spread water out instead of concentrating it.
avoid: Do not send concentrated runoff through loose bare soil.

do: Match plants to light level; woodland-edge species may fit better than prairie species in shade.
Protect tree root zones and leaf litter where appropriate.
avoid: Do not force full-sun prairie plants into deep shade.

do: Check whether the root zone is wet, dry, or compacted before watering again.
Use plants adapted to the actual water pattern.
avoid: Do not keep watering if roots are sitting in saturated soil.

soil_habitat_cards.label: Sticky Clay Prairie Soil
soil_habitat_cards.story: This soil acts like a sponge made of tiny plates. It can hold water and nutrients, but it can get hard, sticky, or compacted.
soil_habitat_cards.root_meaning: Roots need air pockets, slow water, and time. Deep native roots help build structure.
soil_habitat_cards.first_move: Keep soil covered and avoid working it when wet.

soil_habitat_cards.label: Limestone Lunchbox Soil
soil_habitat_cards.story: This soil can have plenty of minerals, but high pH can lock some nutrients away from plants.
soil_habitat_cards.root_meaning: Plants should be adapted to calcium-rich, alkaline conditions.
soil_habitat_cards.first_move: Choose limestone-adapted natives before trying to change the pH.

soil_habitat_cards.label: Thin-Skin Rocky Soil
soil_habitat_cards.story: This soil is a thin blanket over rock. It heats and dries quickly.
soil_habitat_cards.root_meaning: Roots have less room, so plant size and water demand matter.
soil_habitat_cards.first_move: Protect the thin soil layer and use tough local natives.

soil_habitat_cards.label: Flood-Pulse Soil
soil_habitat_cards.story: This soil may get wet enough that air disappears from pore spaces for a while.
soil_habitat_cards.root_meaning: Plants need to tolerate short periods of wet feet if the wetness is real and repeated.
soil_habitat_cards.first_move: Confirm wetness with observation, then choose plants that fit it.

soil_habitat_cards.label: Covered Living Soil
soil_habitat_cards.story: Covered soil stays cooler, loses less water, and feeds more soil life than bare soil.
soil_habitat_cards.root_meaning: Roots and litter become the food and shelter for the soil food web.
soil_habitat_cards.first_move: Keep leaves, mulch, or living plants on the soil surface.

backyard_tests.label: Water soak-in test
backyard_tests.question: How long did water take to soak in?

choices.label: Less than 5 minutes
choices.meaning: Water enters fast. Soil may be sandy, cracked, dry, or well structured.

choices.label: 5-30 minutes
choices.meaning: Moderate soak-in. This is often workable for many native beds.

choices.label: More than 30 minutes
choices.meaning: Slow soak-in. Clay, compaction, crusting, or saturation may be limiting water movement.

choices.label: Still there after 1 hour
choices.meaning: Very slow soak-in or saturated soil. Confirm whether this is compaction, a low spot, or true wet soil.

backyard_tests.how_to: Push a bottomless can or ring into the soil, pour in a measured amount of water, and time how long it takes to disappear.

backyard_tests.label: Ribbon test
backyard_tests.question: What happens when you squeeze moist soil?

choices.label: Falls apart quickly
choices.meaning: Lower clay; water may drain faster and organic cover still matters.

choices.label: Makes a short ribbon
choices.meaning: Moderate clay or loam-clay mix. Good structure is possible with roots and cover.

choices.label: Makes a long sticky ribbon
choices.meaning: High clay. Avoid working it wet and choose clay-tolerant natives.

backyard_tests.how_to: Moisten soil until it feels like putty, squeeze it between thumb and finger, and see whether it forms a ribbon.

backyard_tests.label: Shovel/root-zone test
backyard_tests.question: What do you see in a small hole?

choices.label: Many roots and crumbs
choices.meaning: Good signs: roots and crumbs suggest structure and living soil habitat.

choices.label: Hard layer or plate-like chunks
choices.meaning: Compaction or dense clay may be restricting roots and air.

choices.label: Rock very close to surface
choices.meaning: Shallow soil. Choose plants adapted to thin rocky conditions.

choices.label: Sour smell or gray wet soil
choices.meaning: Low oxygen may be present. Confirm drainage and wetness before planting dry-upland species.

backyard_tests.how_to: Dig one small test hole in a place you can safely disturb. Look for roots, crumbs, hard layers, rock, smell, and moisture.

spring: Plant warm-season natives while moisture is still available.
Watch where storms create runoff, puddles, or crusting.
Mulch or plant cover before heat arrives.
summer: Protect soil from heat with living plants, leaves, or mulch.
Water new plants deeply but less often; check moisture below the surface.
Avoid major soil disturbance during extreme heat.
fall: Best season for many Central Texas native plantings.
Seed or plant prairie species when timing fits the species.
Use fall roots to prepare the soil for next summer.
winter: Plan beds, paths, and plant lists.
Let leaves feed and protect soil where appropriate.

confidence_rules.low: Low: this is based on a goal only. Use the map or one backyard test before making big changes.
confidence_rules.medium: Medium: your observations give useful clues, but construction, fill, irrigation, and compaction can change small sites.
confidence_rules.higher: Higher: mapped soil plus repeated backyard observations point in the same direction. A lab soil test is still needed for fertilizer decisions.
